title: Build Cool Tools Fast
outcome: Find a problem worth solving, build a tool that solves it, get real users, and make it sustainable — repeatedly.

phases.name: Finding Something Worth Building
phases.outcome: Generate, filter and validate tool ideas so you build things people actually use.

modules.name: Where Ideas Actually Come From
modules.objective: Generate tool ideas from observed friction rather than from brainstorming.
lessons: Your own annoyance is the best signal you have
Watching how people work around a missing tool
The spreadsheet that's secretly an application
Ideas from communities you're already in
Keeping an idea log that's worth rereading
practice: Turn eight observed frictions into tool ideas
lab: Log two weeks of friction
An idea log with at least fifteen entries and three candidates marked

modules.name: Finding Out Before You Build
modules.objective: Test whether an idea is wanted before spending weeks on it.
lessons: Nobody will tell you your idea is bad, so ask differently
Asking about behaviour, not about intentions
The existing solution people already put up with
Cheap signals: a landing page, a post, a waitlist
Killing an idea early and cheaply
practice: Design a validation test for seven ideas
lab: Validate one idea before writing code
A validation record with what you asked, who answered, and your go/no-go

modules.name: Cutting It Down to Shippable
modules.objective: Reduce an idea to the smallest version that's genuinely useful.
lessons: The version that's useful in one week
Features to cut, and the one you can't
Manual behind the curtain: faking the hard part
Scoping to a week you might spend in bed
practice: Cut seven bloated specs to a week's work
lab: Scope your tool to a one-week build
A scoped spec with an explicit cut list and the one job it does

modules.name: Who It's For
modules.objective: Define a specific user well enough that design decisions become obvious.
lessons: Designing for the person with no energy today
practice: Sharpen seven vague audience definitions
lab: Write the user definition for your tool
A user definition specific enough to settle three real design arguments

modules.name: What Already Exists
modules.objective: Find what's already out there and decide honestly whether to build anyway.
lessons: Looking properly before assuming nothing exists
Why an existing tool isn't good enough, specifically
Free, open source, and competing with those
Building it anyway for a good reason
Building it anyway for a bad reason
practice: Assess seven ideas against what exists
lab: Do the competitive research on your idea
A written assessment of five existing tools and your specific differentiation

phases.name: Building It Fast
phases.outcome: Get from a scoped idea to something that runs, using AI assistance without losing control.

modules.name: The First Working Version
modules.objective: Get something running end to end before making any part of it good.
lessons: End to end and ugly beats one perfect piece
Hardcoding things you'll fix later, deliberately
The first version's job is to be wrong quickly
Building in sessions that fit your capacity
practice: Plan the thinnest end-to-end slice of seven tools
lab: Build your tool's first working version
Something that runs end to end, however ugly

modules.name: Building With AI Assistance
modules.objective: Use AI tools to build faster without ending up with code you can't change.
lessons: Specifying a feature well enough to delegate it
Reviewing generated code before it compounds
The point where you no longer understand your own project
Building on days when you can't type much
practice: Write specs for seven features to delegate
lab: Build one feature entirely by direction
A working feature plus your review notes on every generated piece

modules.name: Command-Line Tools
modules.objective: Build a command-line tool that other people can install and use.
lessons: When a CLI is the right shape
Output that works in a pipe and for a human
Errors, exit codes and being scriptable
Packaging so someone can actually install it
practice: Design the interface for seven CLI tools
lab: Build and publish a small CLI tool
A published tool someone else can install and run from your README

modules.name: Web Tools
modules.objective: Build a web tool that works on a phone, in bed, for everyone.
lessons: The simplest web tool that could work
State, and keeping it somewhere sensible
Making it usable on a phone one-handed
Accessible from the start, not retrofitted
practice: Design the three states for seven interfaces
lab: Build a web tool that passes an accessibility check
A deployed tool that works keyboard-only and at 400% zoom

modules.name: Tools With AI Inside
modules.objective: Build a tool where a model does part of the work, reliably enough to ship.
lessons: Deciding which step the model should do
Prompts as versioned parts of your codebase
Structured output your code can rely on
What the user sees when the model is wrong
Working when the API is down
practice: Design the AI step and its fallback for seven tools
lab: Build an AI-powered feature with a real fallback
A working feature that degrades gracefully when the model fails or is unavailable

phases.name: Making It Good Enough to Use
phases.outcome: Turn something that runs into something people can rely on.

modules.name: Usability Without a Designer
modules.objective: Make a tool understandable without instructions.
lessons: Watching one person use it without helping them
Defaults that mean nobody has to configure it
Naming things the way users say them
Removing a step versus explaining it
Copy as interface: the words are the design
practice: Improve seven confusing interfaces
lab: Watch someone use your tool and fix what you saw
A record of the session plus the three changes you made because of it

modules.name: Testing What Matters
modules.objective: Test the parts where being wrong actually costs something.
lessons: What to test when you can't test everything
Testing the thing that would embarrass you
Testing AI-powered steps that aren't deterministic
A test that catches the bug you already shipped once
Keeping the suite fast enough to run
practice: Choose what to test for seven tools
lab: Add a focused test suite to your tool
A suite covering the failure cases that would actually cost you users

modules.name: Reliability
modules.objective: Make a tool that keeps working when the world doesn't cooperate.
lessons: Retries, timeouts and giving up properly
Rate limits and what to do at the wall
Failing in a way the user can act on
practice: Handle seven external failure scenarios
lab: Make your tool survive every external failure
A tool tested against a deliberately broken dependency, with the behaviour documented

modules.name: Fast Enough
modules.objective: Find and fix the slowness that users actually feel.
lessons: The one slow thing that's causing all of it
Perceived speed and what to show while waiting
Caching, and the bugs it introduces
Fast enough on a bad phone and a bad connection
practice: Diagnose the bottleneck in seven slow tools
lab: Profile and speed up your tool
Before-and-after measurements with the specific change that caused each improvement

modules.name: Documentation People Read
modules.objective: Write the minimum documentation that makes a tool usable by a stranger.
lessons: The README that gets someone running in a minute
Documenting the thing that confuses everyone
Keeping docs true as the tool changes
Docs as your own memory in six months
practice: Rewrite seven unusable READMEs
lab: Write your tool's documentation and test it
Documentation a stranger successfully followed, with their sticking points fixed

phases.name: Getting It To People
phases.outcome: Launch a tool, find its first users, and learn from what they actually do.

modules.name: Launching
modules.objective: Put a tool in front of people without waiting for it to be finished.
lessons: Where to post it, and how not to be spam
practice: Write launch posts for seven tools
lab: Launch your tool somewhere real
A published launch post and a record of the response

modules.name: The First Ten Users
modules.objective: Get and learn from the small number of people who use it first.
lessons: Ten real users beat a thousand visitors
Asking what they actually did, not what they thought
The feature everyone asks for and nobody uses
Users who use it wrong, which is information
Supporting people without it eating your week
practice: Interpret seven pieces of user feedback
lab: Recruit and interview five users
Five interview records and the three changes you'll make because of them

modules.name: Knowing What's Happening
modules.objective: Measure use in a way that answers a question you actually have.
lessons: Deciding the question before adding tracking
Numbers that don't tell you what to do
practice: Choose the right measurement for seven questions
lab: Instrument your tool to answer one question
Working measurement plus the answer it gave you after a week

modules.name: Changing It Without Breaking It
modules.objective: Decide what to change next and ship it without breaking existing users.
lessons: Deciding what to build next, with evidence
Saying no to a feature request kindly
Knowing when the tool is done
practice: Prioritise seven feature backlogs
lab: Ship one evidence-driven change
A shipped change with the evidence that prompted it and the effect measured

modules.name: People Around the Tool
modules.objective: Handle users, contributors and the social side without it consuming you.
lessons: Being the maintainer of something people rely on
Issues, requests and expectations you set
Handing a project over, or archiving it honestly
practice: Draft responses to seven maintainer situations
lab: Write your project's contribution and support policy
A policy stating response times, scope and what you won't do

phases.name: Making It Sustainable
phases.outcome: Cover costs, charge if you want to, and run a tool that doesn't cost you more than it gives.

modules.name: What It Costs to Run
modules.objective: Know what a tool costs you monthly, and what happens if it gets popular.
lessons: Hosting, storage and bandwidth in real numbers
AI usage costs at ten and ten thousand users
Free tiers and the cliff at the end
Setting a spending limit before you need one
practice: Model the cost curve for seven tools
lab: Build a cost model for your tool
A cost model at three usage levels with a spending cap actually configured

modules.name: Charging for It
modules.objective: Decide whether and how to charge, and set a price you can defend.
lessons: Free, paid, freemium: what each one commits you to
Pricing: what you can defend, not what feels comfortable
Pricing for people who don't have much money
What paying users are entitled to expect
practice: Set and defend a price for seven tools
lab: Add payment to your tool
Working payment with a written pricing rationale and a refund policy

modules.name: The Legal Minimum
modules.objective: Know what you're obliged to have before other people use your tool.
lessons: Terms and privacy policy: what they're actually for
Personal data and the obligations it creates
Choosing a licence for your code
Liability when your tool gets something wrong
practice: Identify the legal gap in seven launches
lab: Get your tool legally ready to launch
Terms, privacy policy and licence in place, each one you can explain

modules.name: Tools as Proof
modules.objective: Turn shipped tools into evidence that gets you work.
lessons: What a shipped tool proves that a course doesn't
Writing up a build so people read it
Turning a tool into paid work
Three shipped tools as a career argument
practice: Rewrite seven project write-ups
lab: Write the build story of your tool
A published write-up covering problem, decisions, mistakes and results

modules.name: Capstone — Idea to Users
modules.objective: Take one new idea through the entire cycle: validate, build, launch, learn.
lessons: Building to a fixed, honest scope
practice: Pressure-test seven capstone plans
lab: Deliver the capstone tool
A launched tool with validation evidence, real users, measured use and an honest retrospective

phases.name: Doing It Again, Better
phases.outcome: Build a repeatable practice rather than a single lucky project.

modules.name: Your Own Toolkit
modules.objective: Build the reusable pieces that make the next tool much faster.
lessons: The things you rebuild every time
A starter template that's actually yours
Keeping the toolkit from becoming a burden
practice: Identify the reusable pieces in seven projects
lab: Build your project starter template
A template that gets a new project running with tests and deploy in under an hour

modules.name: Getting Genuinely Faster
modules.objective: Reduce the time from idea to shipped without cutting the parts that matter.
lessons: Decisions made once, not per project
practice: Find the time sink in seven build logs
lab: Time one build and analyse where it went
A time log with your three biggest sinks and what you'll change

modules.name: Running Several Things
modules.objective: Maintain more than one live tool without drowning.
lessons: The maintenance cost of each live thing
Automating the boring parts of ownership
How many live projects you can actually carry
practice: Triage seven project portfolios
lab: Audit and prune your own project portfolio
A portfolio audit with a keep/automate/archive decision per project

modules.name: Building With Someone Else
modules.objective: Work with a collaborator without meetings or matching schedules.
lessons: Splitting work so nobody blocks anybody
Writing decisions down instead of discussing them
Agreeing what happens when someone can't work
practice: Resolve seven collaboration breakdowns
lab: Write a collaboration agreement
An agreement covering scope, decisions, review, capacity and exit

modules.name: The Long Game
modules.objective: Build a body of work over years at whatever pace your body allows.
lessons: What a decade of small tools adds up to
Building a reputation without performing constantly
Coming back after a long gap
Deciding what you actually want this for
practice: Assess seven project paths for compounding value
lab: Write your own two-year plan
A plan with a direction, three projects and an explicit pace you can sustain
